title: Arrays & Dynamic Arrays
summary: Arrays are the most fundamental data structure in computer science. Starting from how data is stored in memory, we explore how dynamic arrays overcome the limitations of static arrays — and why append is effectively O(1) through amortized analysis.

blocks.content: Imagine managing scores for 100 students without arrays. You'd write: score1 = 85, score2 = 92, ... score100 = 88. You'd declare 100 separate variables, couldn't use loops, and computing the average would mean adding 100 variables by hand. That's the world before arrays.

Arrays solve this by grouping data under numbered slots: scores[0], scores[1], ..., scores[99]. Now a single loop handles 100 scores. The core idea: 'store same-kind data in a numbered, contiguous block.'

items: Without arrays: n separate variables → no loops, no maintainability
With arrays: manage n items by index as a single unit
Array = same-type data stored consecutively with numbered positions
Real-world analogy: apartment unit numbers — rooms in one building, each uniquely numbered

blocks.python:
# Without arrays (bad)
score1 = 85
score2 = 92
score3 = 78
average = (score1 + score2 + score3) / 3

# With arrays (good)
scores = [85, 92, 78, 91, 88]
average = sum(scores) / len(scores)
print(f'Average: {average}')  # 86.8

blocks.content: To truly understand arrays, you need to know how RAM works. Think of RAM as a massive locker room with billions of numbered lockers in a row. Each locker holds exactly 1 byte of data and has a unique address.

When you declare an array, the OS reserves a contiguous block of lockers. Declaring an int array of 5 elements reserves 4 bytes × 5 = 20 consecutive lockers. This contiguity is the key property of arrays.

blocks.alt: Memory layout of a 5-element int array — addresses 1000 through 1019, 20 bytes contiguous

blocks.content: The address of the first element is called the Base Address. Any element's address is: Base + index × element_size. For arr[3]: 1000 + 3 × 4 = 1012. This trivial arithmetic runs in O(1), which is why random access is instant regardless of array size.

items: RAM = numbered lockers, each holding 1 byte
Array declaration = requesting N contiguous lockers from the OS
Base Address: address of the first element
arr[i] address = Base Address + i × sizeof(element type)
This simple arithmetic enables O(1) access to any position

blocks.content: Most languages index arrays from 0, not 1. It feels unintuitive at first, but the address formula makes the reason clear.

In arr[i] = Base + i × size, the first element's offset from Base must be 0: arr[0] = Base + 0 × size = Base. If indexing started at 1, the formula becomes Base + (i-1) × size — an extra subtraction every time. 0-based indexing keeps the math as simple as possible.

items: Index = offset (distance from the base), so first element has offset 0
0-based: arr[0] = Base + 0, no subtraction needed
1-based would require: Base + (i-1) × size — more complex
C, C++, Java, Python, JavaScript all use 0-based indexing
Python supports negative indices: arr[-1] is the last element

blocks.python:
arr = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]

print(arr[0])   # 10 (first)
print(arr[4])   # 50 (last, max index = len-1 = 4)
print(arr[-1])  # 50 (Python: negative index from end)
print(arr[-2])  # 40

# Valid range: 0 ~ len(arr)-1
# arr[5] raises IndexError!

steps.title: Core Operations — Access, Search, Insert, Delete

blocks.content: Arrays support four fundamental operations: Access, Search, Insert, and Delete. Each has a different time complexity, and understanding these is essential to using arrays correctly.
Access: arr[i] reaches any element directly via the address formula — O(1) regardless of array size. This is the array's greatest strength.
Search: Finding a value in an unsorted array requires checking each element (linear search) — O(n) worst case. A sorted array allows binary search — O(log n).
Insert: Appending to the end is O(1). Inserting in the middle requires shifting all subsequent elements one position right — O(n) in the worst case (inserting at position 0 shifts every element).

blocks.alt: Array mid-insertion: inserting 15 at index 1 in [10,20,30,40] — arrows show 20/30/40 each shifting one slot right, resulting in [10,15,20,30,40]

blocks.content: Delete: Removing from the end is O(1). Removing from the middle requires shifting subsequent elements left to fill the gap — O(n) worst case.

blocks.python:
arr = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]

# 1. Access O(1)
print(arr[2])  # 30

# 2. Linear Search O(n)
def linear_search(arr, target):
    for i, val in enumerate(arr):
        if val == target:
            return i
    return -1
print(linear_search(arr, 30))  # 2

# 3. Mid-insert O(n) — internal shifting
arr.insert(2, 99)
print(arr)  # [10, 20, 99, 30, 40, 50]

# 4. Delete O(n)
arr.pop(2)  # remove index 2
print(arr)  # [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]

blocks.content: The arrays discussed so far are static arrays — their size must be fixed at declaration and cannot change. This is the primary limitation.

When you don't know how many items to store, you face a dilemma. Too small: overflow when data exceeds capacity. Too large: wasted memory for unused slots. 3 items in a 1000-slot array wastes 997 slots.

items: Limitation 1 — Fixed size: can't grow. Need a new array + manual copy when full
Limitation 2 — Memory waste: reserving extra space wastes memory
Limitation 3 — Costly mid-insert/delete: O(n) element shifting
Limitation 4 — Must know size in advance: hard to design when count is unknown at runtime

blocks.python:
# Simulating static array overflow
MAX_SIZE = 5
arr = [0] * MAX_SIZE
size = 0

def add(value):
    global size
    if size >= MAX_SIZE:
        print('Array full! Cannot add more.')
        return
    arr[size] = value
    size += 1

add(10); add(20); add(30); add(40); add(50)
add(60)  # Prints: 'Array full! Cannot add more.'

blocks.content: Dynamic arrays solve static array limitations by separating the logical size (how many elements are stored) from the physical capacity (how much space is reserved).

Restaurant analogy: a restaurant has 20 seats but only 8 customers. size = 8, capacity = 20. New customers take empty seats. When all seats fill up, you bring more tables — just like a dynamic array automatically allocates more space when capacity is exceeded.

blocks.alt: Dynamic array capacity vs size — 8-slot internal array with 3 filled (size=3, capacity=8). Filled slots shown as solid blue boxes, empty slots as dashed gray boxes. Arrows below mark the size range and capacity range

items: size: number of elements actually stored (logical size)
capacity: total memory reserved internally (physical size)
Always: size ≤ capacity
Python list, Java ArrayList, C++ vector, C# List<T>, JavaScript Array are all dynamic arrays
In most languages, dynamic arrays behave as the default array type

blocks.python:
import sys

arr = []  # Python list = dynamic array

for i in range(9):
    arr.append(i)
    print(f'size={len(arr)}, allocated_bytes={sys.getsizeof(arr)}')

# A jump in bytes marks a resize event!
# 0→56, 1→88, 5→120, 9→184 (CPython)

blocks.content: Resizing is the core mechanism of dynamic arrays. When size reaches capacity, three steps execute automatically.

items: Step 1 — Allocate new array: create a new array with 2× (or 1.5×) the current capacity in memory
Step 2 — Copy data: copy every element from the old array to the new one — this costs O(n)
Step 3 — Swap reference: point the dynamic array to the new internal array; release the old memory

blocks.alt: 3-step resizing diagram — Step 1: [A,B,C,D] capacity=4 is full, E requested (arrow). Step 2: new capacity=8 array created below, A/B/C/D copied with arrows. Step 3: result [A,B,C,D,E,_,_,_] size=5 capacity=8

blocks.content: Why double? Smaller growth (e.g. 1.1×) causes too-frequent resizing. Larger growth (e.g. 3×) wastes memory. Doubling (or 1.5×) balances resize frequency against memory overhead. This multiplier is called the growth factor.

items: Growth Factor: new capacity = old capacity × growth factor
Python list: ~1.125–2× (complex formula, grows more when small)
Java ArrayList: 1.5× (oldCapacity + oldCapacity >> 1)
C++ std::vector: 2× (GCC/Clang; may vary by implementation)
C# List<T>: 2×
Larger growth factor → more wasted memory, fewer resizes

steps.title: Amortized Analysis — Why Append Is O(1)

blocks.content: Resizing costs O(n); ordinary appends cost O(1). So what is the time complexity of append? The answer is 'O(1) amortized.' Amortized analysis proves this.

Amortized analysis distributes the cost of expensive operations across many cheap ones. Bank account analogy: each cheap O(1) append deposits a small credit toward the future resize cost. When a resize occurs, those credits pay the bill.
The math: for n appends with capacity doubling (1→2→4→...→n), total copies = 1+2+4+...+n/2 = n-1. Total cost for n appends = O(n). Average cost per append = O(n)/n = O(1).

blocks.alt: Amortized analysis bar chart — x-axis: append number (1–16), y-axis: actual cost. Most operations cost 1 (short bars), but appends 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 spike with resize cost (tall bars). Dashed horizontal line at y=2 shows the amortized average

items: Amortized O(1): worst case is O(n), but average over n operations is O(1)
Resizing happens only at sizes 1, 2, 4, 8, 16... — log₂n times total
Total copies = 1+2+4+...+n/2 = n-1, average ≈ 1 per append
append: O(1) amortized / O(n) worst case (when resize triggers)
Interview tip: 'almost always O(1), occasional O(n) spikes that average out'

blocks.content: Each language names and uses its dynamic array slightly differently. Here is a practical summary of the most commonly used methods.

blocks.python:
arr = []  # or list()

# Add
arr.append(10)        # append to end O(1) amortized
arr.insert(1, 99)     # insert at index O(n)
arr.extend([20, 30])  # append multiple

# Remove
arr.pop()             # remove last O(1)
arr.pop(0)            # remove at index O(n)
arr.remove(99)        # remove first match O(n)

# Search
print(99 in arr)      # O(n)
print(arr.index(10))  # O(n)

# Slicing
print(arr[1:3])       # subarray O(k)
print(arr[::-1])      # reversed copy O(n)

print(len(arr))       # size
blocks.javascript:
const arr = [];

arr.push(10, 20);         // append O(1) amortized
arr.unshift(5);           // prepend O(n)
arr.splice(1, 0, 99);     // insert at index O(n)

arr.pop();                // remove last O(1)
arr.shift();              // remove first O(n)
arr.splice(1, 1);         // remove at index O(n)

console.log(arr.includes(10));       // O(n)
console.log(arr.indexOf(10));        // O(n)
console.log(arr.find(x => x > 5));   // O(n)

const copy = arr.slice(1, 3);        // subarray
console.log(arr.length);             // size

steps.title: Time Complexity Summary — When to Use Arrays

blocks.content: Here is the complete time complexity reference for all array operations. Understanding best, average, and worst cases is key.

items: Access arr[i]: O(1) — always constant, the array's biggest strength
Search (unsorted): O(n) — linear scan
Search (sorted + binary search): O(log n)
Append (push to end): O(1) amortized / O(n) worst case (resize)
Insert at middle or front: O(n) — element shifting
Delete last element: O(1)
Delete at middle or front: O(n) — element shifting
Space complexity: O(n) — dynamic arrays may use up to 2n slots due to capacity

blocks.content: Arrays vs Linked Lists: Arrays excel at O(1) access but pay O(n) for mid-insert/delete. Linked lists flip this — O(1) mid-insert/delete but O(n) access. Choose based on your dominant operation.

items: Prefer arrays when: frequent index-based access, append-only, or binary search on sorted data
Prefer linked lists when: frequent mid-insert/delete or rapidly changing size
Practical rule: dynamic array (list/ArrayList/vector) is the default first choice
Arrays also win on cache efficiency — contiguous memory is CPU-cache friendly vs linked list pointer chasing

steps.title: Practical Patterns — Two Pointers and Prefix Sum

blocks.content: Two essential array-based patterns appear in countless coding problems. Mastering them lets you solve many problems efficiently.

Pattern 1 — Two Pointers: Place two index pointers at different positions and move them toward each other based on a condition. Reduces O(n²) brute-force to O(n) for problems like 'find two numbers in a sorted array that sum to target.'
Pattern 2 — Prefix Sum: Precompute cumulative sums so any range sum query answers in O(1). Transforms O(n²) into O(n + q) where q is the number of queries.

blocks.python:
# Two Pointers — find pair summing to target in sorted array
def two_sum_sorted(arr, target):
    left, right = 0, len(arr) - 1
    while left < right:
        s = arr[left] + arr[right]
        if s == target:   return (left, right)
        elif s < target:  left += 1
        else:             right -= 1
    return None

print(two_sum_sorted([1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11], 10))  # (1, 3) → 3+7

# Prefix Sum — range sum in O(1)
def build_prefix(arr):
    p = [0] * (len(arr) + 1)
    for i, v in enumerate(arr):
        p[i + 1] = p[i] + v
    return p

def range_sum(p, l, r):  # sum of arr[l..r]
    return p[r + 1] - p[l]

arr = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6]
p = build_prefix(arr)
print(range_sum(p, 2, 5))  # 4+1+5+9 = 19

blocks.content: The best way to master arrays is to solve problems. Here are recommended resources organized by learning stage.

items: [ Visualization ] VisuAlgo (visualgo.net) — step-by-step animation of arrays, sorting, and search. Great for seeing insert/delete shifts in action
[ Theory ] GeeksforGeeks — Array Data Structure (geeksforgeeks.org/array-data-structure) — comprehensive coverage with code examples
[ Practice — Beginner ] LeetCode (leetcode.com) — Array tag, Easy level. Start with: Two Sum (#1), Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock (#121), Maximum Subarray (#53)
[ Practice — Intermediate ] LeetCode Medium: Container With Most Water (#11), 3Sum (#15), Product of Array Except Self (#238)
[ Practice — Korean ] Baekjoon Online Judge (acmicpc.net) — 'Array' tag. Start with: 10818 (Min/Max), 2562 (Max value), 1330 (Compare two numbers)
[ Book ] 'Introduction to Algorithms' (CLRS) — Chapter on sorting and arrays for deep theoretical foundation

blocks.content: Recommended study order: Arrays → Linked Lists → Stack & Queue → Hash Table. Understanding arrays first makes the contrast with linked lists immediately clear: 'Array = contiguous memory + fast access, Linked List = scattered memory + flexible insert/delete.' Remember this tradeoff — it comes up in every data structures interview.
